s: Forbes America's Richest Self-Made Women, 3 Jun 2025, rank 82
m: Published Forbes list figure; her Hello Sunshine stake marked off the 900 million dollar valuation Blackstone-backed Candle Media paid in Aug 2021
did: Started the production company Pacific Standard in 2012 with Bruna Papandrea, optioned Wild and Gone Girl before either was a hit, rebranded it Hello Sunshine in 2016 around Big Little Lies and The Morning Show, and sold it to Blackstone-backed Candle Media in Aug 2021 at a 900 million dollar valuation.
why: She bought book rights before publication and then used her book club to manufacture demand for the same titles she already controlled. That made her the cheapest source of proven female-led IP exactly when Netflix, Apple and Hulu were bidding for it, so buyers came to her.
obst: Studios passed on both Wild and Gone Girl as unfinanceable female-led projects, so Pacific Standard optioned the books itself with no distributor attached and Wild was made for roughly 15 million dollars with Witherspoon funding development personally.
turn: 2014, when Wild and Gone Girl both reached cinemas from books she had optioned cheaply, proving the pipeline and letting her raise outside capital to build Hello Sunshine.

s: Los Angeles Business Journal Wealthiest Angelenos issue, 6 Oct 2025, citing Forbes
m: Forbes figure of 300 million dollars as reported by the LABJ; anchored to e.l.f. Beauty's 2025 purchase of Rhode for up to 1 billion dollars
did: Launched the skincare line Rhode in June 2022 with three products sold only on its own website, held it out of wholesale for three years, put it into Sephora in 2025 and sold it to e.l.f. Beauty the same year for up to 1 billion dollars while staying on as chief creative officer.
why: Refusing wholesale kept the full retail margin and the first-party customer data inside the company, and her own audience removed paid acquisition entirely. A brand with no distribution partner and no ad budget showed e.l.f. margins no conventional beauty startup could match.
obst: She launched into a celebrity-beauty field already littered with failures such as KKW Beauty and Item Beauty, and was sued in 2022 by the founders of the fashion label Rhode over the name; a judge denied their injunction and the case later settled.
turn: The June 2022 launch of the peptide lip treatment, which drew a waitlist in the hundreds of thousands and sold out repeatedly, making scarcity the entire marketing model.

s: Guess?, Inc. DEFM14A filed 21 Oct 2025; Authentic Brands take-private at 16.75 dollars per share
m: 14,876,944 shares beneficially owned at the 20 Oct 2025 record date times the 16.75 dollar merger price equals 249 million dollars; he rolled the equity into the buyer rather than cashing out
did: Left Marseille for Los Angeles and founded Guess with his brothers in 1981 around a stonewashed three-zip Marilyn jean, then ran creative and advertising for four decades, shooting the black-and-white campaigns that launched Claudia Schiffer and Anna Nicole Smith. He held 28 percent at the 2025 take-private.
why: Guess kept advertising in-house and shot denim like fashion editorial, so a commodity garment carried a designer price. Licensing watches, fragrance and eyewear then turned the logo into royalty income that kept paying when the apparel cycle turned against it.
obst: A decade of litigation with the Nakash brothers of Jordache, who bought half of Guess in 1983 and fought the Marcianos for control until a 1990 settlement, and a 2018 board investigation into misconduct allegations that stripped him of executive authority while he kept the creative role and his stake.
turn: The first order in 1981, when Bloomingdale's agreed to take two dozen pairs of the Marilyn jean as a test and sold them out the same day.

s: Revolve Group DEF 14A filed 24 Apr 2026; RVLV close of 23.76 dollars on 21 Aug 2026
m: MMMK Development holds 30,107,847 Class B shares and he and Mente are its only two stockholders; half of that plus his 123,000 Class A shares at 23.76 dollars equals 361 million dollars
did: Co-founded the online fashion retailer Revolve in a Los Angeles apartment in 2003 with Michael Mente, writing the merchandising, pricing and returns software himself, and took it to roughly 1.1 billion dollars of net sales and a June 2019 IPO while the two of them still held about 88 percent of the voting power.
why: He built the buying system instead of buying it. Revolve reads sell-through and return reasons at SKU level daily, so it orders shallow and reorders fast, which is why it holds full-price margin in a category where Shopbop and Farfetch discount their way through every season.
obst: They raised almost no outside capital, so a credit line pulled in 2008 nearly ended the company; and from 2022 the aspirational-luxury slowdown cut Revolve's share price roughly 80 percent from its peak while they held the stock.
turn: The 2015 decision to move the marketing budget almost entirely into paying influencers in product and travel, starting with the first Revolve Festival at Coachella.

s: Revolve Group DEF 14A filed 24 Apr 2026; RVLV close of 23.76 dollars on 21 Aug 2026
m: Half of MMMK Development's 30,107,847 Class B shares, which he and Karanikolas jointly and solely own, plus his 35,331 direct Class B and 73,000 Class A shares, at 23.76 dollars equals 360 million dollars
did: Co-founded Revolve with Mike Karanikolas in 2003, running buying and brand while Karanikolas built the systems; he added the luxury site FWRD in 2018, took the company public in June 2019 at 18 dollars a share, and still owns half of MMMK Development, which holds nearly all of Revolve's Class B stock.
why: Revolve stocked hundreds of small emerging labels rather than a few large ones, so no single brand could dictate terms or undercut it elsewhere. Owning the assortment rather than licensing a marketplace is what made the influencer spend actually convert into orders.
obst: Revolve began by clearing other retailers' surplus inventory and had to spend years convincing designers it was not a discounter; the 2022 to 2024 downturn then cut growth to near zero and the share price by about 80 percent.
turn: The June 2019 IPO, which closed its first day up 89 percent and marked the founders' stake in the billions without either of them having sold control.

s: Houlihan Lokey DEF 14A filed 24 Jul 2026, ownership as of 23 Jul 2026; HLI close of 129.05 dollars on 21 Aug 2026
m: 1,061,766 shares held by The Gold Stock Trust over which he has disposition power, at 129.05 dollars, equals 137 million dollars; excludes the wider HL Voting Trust he disclaims
did: Joined Houlihan Lokey in 1988 and founded its financial restructuring group, which became the busiest bankruptcy advisory practice on Wall Street and took the Lehman Brothers creditor mandate in 2008; he was co-chairman through the 2015 IPO and is now executive chairman of the board.
why: Restructuring fees peak exactly when merger fees collapse, so pairing the two inside one mid-cap firm produced revenue that did not fall in 2001 or 2008. Bulge-bracket banks could not copy it because advising creditors conflicts with lending to the same companies.
obst: Building a creditor-side advisory business inside a small Los Angeles valuation shop when every large bankruptcy mandate went to New York, then negotiating the buyback from ORIX, the Japanese owner since 2006, to make a 2015 listing possible.
turn: The 2008 to 2009 credit crisis, when the group he built won the Lehman Brothers creditors mandate and firm fee income rose while advisory rivals halved.

s: Houlihan Lokey DEF 14A filed 24 Jul 2026, ownership as of 23 Jul 2026; HLI close of 129.05 dollars on 21 Aug 2026
m: 885,102 shares held by the Adelson Stock Trust over which he has disposition power, at 129.05 dollars, equals 114 million dollars; excludes the wider HL Voting Trust he disclaims
did: Joined Houlihan Lokey in 1987, built its corporate finance and industrials practice and its business of selling founder-owned mid-market companies, served as global co-head of corporate finance, and became chief executive of the firm in 2021.
why: Houlihan chased the deals too small for bulge brackets to staff, where the seller is a founder who has never sold anything and pays for hand-holding rather than balance sheet. Volume in that segment made it the most active M&A adviser in the world by deal count.
obst: Persuading a firm known for valuations and fairness opinions that it could actually sell companies, then holding mid-market bankers together through the 2015 IPO when public pay discipline replaced private partnership payouts.
turn: The August 2015 IPO at 21 dollars a share, which gave Houlihan acquisition currency it spent on GCA and others and pushed it to number one by global M&A deal count.

s: Houlihan Lokey DEF 14A filed 24 Jul 2026, ownership as of 23 Jul 2026; HLI close of 129.05 dollars on 21 Aug 2026
m: 787,651 shares held by The Beiser Stock Trust over which he has disposition power, at 129.05 dollars, equals 102 million dollars; excludes the wider HL Voting Trust he disclaims
did: Joined Houlihan Lokey in 1983 when it was a Los Angeles valuation firm of a few dozen people, became chief executive in 2003 and ran it until 2021, taking it public in 2015 and past 2 billion dollars of revenue; he is now co-chairman.
why: He kept the firm employee-owned and paid bankers in equity through the ORIX years, so senior people stayed across two downturns. In advisory work continuity is the product, because clients hire the individual, and Houlihan lost fewer of them than any listed rival.
obst: Taking the chief executive job in 2003 under Japanese ownership after ORIX bought control, then negotiating the buyback and convincing a partnership private for four decades to accept public disclosure and lockups in 2015.
turn: The 2006 ORIX recapitalisation, which put capital behind international expansion and set up the 2015 IPO that made the partners' stakes liquid.

s: PayPal's 800 million dollar cash acquisition of Braintree, Dec 2013; his 300 million dollar share reported by Fortune and in his own writing
m: Reported 300 million dollar pre-tax share of the Braintree sale, less the roughly 200 million dollars he has said he put into OS Fund and Kernel, both still held as illiquid assets rather than spent
did: Founded the payments processor Braintree in 2007 while finishing an MBA, selling card processing door to door; it became the payment layer for Uber, Airbnb and OpenTable, bought Venmo for 26.2 million dollars in 2012, and PayPal paid 800 million dollars cash for it in December 2013.
why: Marketplaces could not legally onboard thousands of small sellers themselves. Braintree's single API absorbed sub-merchant underwriting and compliance, so a startup could take payments in dozens of countries on day one, which is why Uber and Airbnb picked it over incumbent gateways.
obst: No processor would sign him as a reseller, so he bootstrapped Braintree past 10 million dollars of revenue before raising a dollar, running it alongside a full-time job and graduate school for its first two years.
turn: Buying Venmo for 26.2 million dollars in 2012, which handed PayPal the consumer network it lacked and roughly doubled what it paid a year later.

s: Wall Street Journal valuation of Primary Wave's December 2020 purchase of 80 percent of her songwriting catalogue at 100 million dollars
m: 100 million dollars for 80 percent implies about 125 million for the whole catalogue; net worth taken as after-tax proceeds plus the retained 20 percent and touring income, not a published list figure
did: Joined Fleetwood Mac with Lindsey Buckingham at the end of 1974 and wrote Rhiannon, Dreams and Landslide, keeping the songwriting credits; in December 2020 she sold 80 percent of her roughly 500-song catalogue to Primary Wave in a deal the Wall Street Journal valued at 100 million dollars.
why: She wrote her own material when most women fronting rock bands sang other people's, so she owned publishing rather than only an artist royalty. Dreams is Fleetwood Mac's only US number one and it is hers, which is why a 45-year-old catalogue repriced upward in 2020.
obst: A cocaine habit that destroyed her septum, then eight years on Klonopin prescribed to treat it, which she has said cost her most of the 1990s; Rumours itself was cut while her relationship with Buckingham and the McVies' marriage were collapsing.
turn: Autumn 2020, when a TikTok clip pushed Dreams back onto the charts weeks before she signed the Primary Wave deal, repricing the catalogue at the moment of sale.

s: Forbes America's Richest Self-Made Women 2021, rank 91, the last edition in which she was ranked
m: Dated Forbes list figure for a wholly owned private company; carried forward unchanged because California Baby has neither raised outside capital nor been sold since
did: Started making shampoo in her Los Angeles kitchen in 1995 after reading the ingredient label on her infant son's bath products, built California Baby into a natural baby-care line sold through Whole Foods and Target, and still owns it outright including its own Los Angeles manufacturing plant.
why: She took no outside capital and built her own factory, so she controlled formulation and could certify claims contract manufacturers could not. That made California Baby the default paediatrician and eczema-forum recommendation years before mass brands had a clean-label answer.
obst: Retail buyers refused a premium-priced baby wash from an unknown founder with no marketing budget, so she sold it store by store; she later had to build her own plant because no contract manufacturer would run preservative-free formulas at her volumes.
turn: Winning national distribution through Whole Foods and then Target, which moved a kitchen-table formula into mass retail without a single advertisement.

s: Forbes America's Richest Self-Made Women 2021, rank 100, the last edition in which she was ranked
m: Dated Forbes list figure; Meaningful Beauty is private and she has not sold a controlling stake, so the figure is carried forward rather than remarked
did: Converted a modelling career built on Vogue covers and the 1992 Pepsi Super Bowl spot into equity by launching the skincare line Meaningful Beauty with Guthy-Renker in 2004 on an infomercial and auto-ship subscription model, which has since sold well over a billion dollars of product.
why: Models rented their names for a flat licence fee. She took an ownership stake and a direct-response subscription channel instead, so revenue recurred monthly and stopped depending on her continuing to be photographed at all.
obst: She was 38 and effectively off the runway when she started, in a category where celebrity skincare was dismissed as a licensing deal, and the infomercial channel she chose carried a downmarket stigma department-store brands used against her.
turn: The 2004 decision to take equity in Meaningful Beauty with Guthy-Renker rather than the flat endorsement fee she was offered.
